extraction.name: CIFAR-10
extraction.description: A labeled subset of the tiny images dataset containing 6000 examples each of 10 classes, created to enable reliable object recognition experiments. It is a collection of 32x32 colour images drawn from a larger dataset of 80 million tiny images collected from the web.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The tiny images dataset was collected by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using multiple search engines. A labeled subset (CIFAR-10) was created by paying students to label images, filtering out mislabeled ones from the tiny images dataset based on search terms and their hyponyms.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Perfect duplicates and images with excessively large portions of white pixels were removed. Duplicate images in the labeled subset were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: 80 million colour images downscaled to 32x32 pixels, collected via web search for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet, spread across 79000 search terms.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human labelers created two sets of reliable labels (CIFAR-10 with 6000 examples per class across 10 classes, and CIFAR-100 with 600 examples per class across 100 non-overlapping classes) from the tiny images dataset. An instruction sheet was provided to labelers (Appendix C: Labeler instruction sheet).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Search engine queries (Google, Flickr, Altavista) provided rough labels via search terms used to find images, though these were noted as extremely unreliable.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images were divided into 8x8 patches (25 patches plus a 26th subsampled patch) for training separate RBMs; RBMs trained on patches were merged into a single large RBM with 7800 hidden units; training was performed on subsets of approximately 2 million images from the full 80 million image dataset.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were whitened using ZCA whitening transformation to remove second-order correlations between pixels. Additionally, the 1000 least-significant principal components (directions of variance) were deleted from the dataset to reduce high-frequency noise. Perfect duplicates and images with excessively large portions of white pixels were removed during original dataset collection.

name.evidence: The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes

description.evidence: The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes. Using these labels, we show that object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images.

They used several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: They used several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term... We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white, as they tended to be synthetic figures rather than natural images. We removed duplicate images from the dataset by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: In total, the dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32 × 32 and spread out across 79000 search terms.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The tiny images dataset on which we based all of our experiments was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We created two sets of reliable labels. The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: We divided the 32x32 images into 25 8x8 patches as shown in Figure 2.4. In addition to the patches shown in Figure 2.4, we created a 26th patch: an 8x8 subsampled version of the entire 32x32 image. We trained 26 independent RBMs with 300 hidden units on each of these patches... Most of our experiments with unsupervised learning were performed on a subset of about 2 million images.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: One way to force the model to ignore second-order structure is to remove it. Luckily this can be done with a data preprocessing step that just consists of multiplying the data matrix by a whitening matrix... we decided to remove some of the least significant directions of variance from the dataset.
